headers.//: BUILD ARTEFACTS — cached for a year, and it is safe. Vite writes a content hash into every filename (index-y4UH__tA.js), so the URL changes whenever the bytes change. A stale file can therefore never be served: a new deploy produces new URLs and the old ones are simply never requested again. This is the exact case `immutable` exists for. Before this, /assets/* fell through to the Express static handler's maxAge:'1h', so a visitor returning the next day re-downloaded the whole 660 KB entry payload — every time. On a slow or congested connection that is most of the wait the owner reported.

FONTS — same reasoning, but the filenames are NOT hashed (Vazirmatn-var.woff2). A year is still right because a variable font is replaced by editing index.html to point somewhere else, not by swapping the bytes under the same name. At ~70 KB for the Persian font this is the single biggest repeat-visit saving after the JS.

ICONS AND MANIFEST — a week, not a year. These are unhashed and DO get replaced in place when the branding changes, so a year would leave a stale icon on home screens with no way to force a refresh. A week is long enough that they are effectively free on repeat visits and short enough that a fix propagates.

index.html — MUST NOT be cached. It is the one file that names the current hashed asset URLs, so caching it pins a returning visitor to the previous deploy's JS. That is how a user ends up on an old build for hours after a fix ships, which is worse than a slow load. must-revalidate makes the browser check every time; the check is a few hundred bytes and usually answers 304.

The service worker, for the same reason and more urgently. A cached sw.js keeps serving its own cached app shell, so a stale one can pin a user to an old build indefinitely — long after index.html has moved on.
